metadata.title: Claude, Google Drive API.
metadata.topic: GOOGLE DRIVE API · CLAUDE TAG PLUGIN
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude finds a Drive file by walking a folder path or by ID, using the Google Drive API skill's own documented facts as the concrete case. Lands the carry-out that every call turns on three habits — folder-as-file, supportsAllDrives, and export instead of download.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (spreadsheets-modified-on-shared-drive-exported-as-csv request, traced through the three shared-drive parameters + fields=nextPageToken, then paid off against export vs alt=media)

beats.narration_text: The natural guess: Drive is a filesystem, so Claude walks folder paths to your file. Wrong model. There's no path API — the whole thing is addressed by ID. What did Google buy with that choice?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude finds my file by its folder path in Drive. Right?', hesitates on 'path', corrects to 'ID', lands the real question

props.text:
Claude finds my file
by its folder path
in Drive. Right?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('path' -> 'ID') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening: a folder in Drive isn't a separate entity. It's a file with a mimeType saying folder. Ask Claude to list its contents and there's no get-folder endpoint to call. It runs a search — every file whose parents array contains that folder's ID. One primitive doing double duty. Costs you a query for what a filesystem gives you free; buys you a graph, where the same file can live under multiple parents at once.

shot.new_visual_element: A 'get folder' endpoint guess struck through; the real query revealed — files filtered by parents containing an ID

production_viz.label: Not a separate thing — a file with a mimeType
production_viz.mechanic: A folder icon and a file icon drawn as two separate shapes, then merged into one card labelled mimeType: "folder". A guessed call 'GET /folders/{id}/contents' fades in above, then gets struck through in terracotta. Beside it, the real query opens: files where parents contains that ID.

beats.narration_text: Say you want every spreadsheet modified this month on your team's shared drive, exported as CSV. Two failure modes hiding in that one request. Shared-drive files are invisible by default — the API was built around personal Drives, and shared drives are opt-in territory. Three parameters just to see them: corpora=allDrives, includeItemsFromAllDrives=true, supportsAllDrives=true. And fields= has to name nextPageToken explicitly, or results quietly stop at page one. They optimized for cheap default responses; you pay for it in silent truncation.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — the shared-drive spreadsheet-export request, three-param requirement and fields=nextPageToken both flagged

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — shared drive, invisible by default
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A request card appears — 'spreadsheets modified this month, on our shared drive, export as CSV'. A shared-drive icon sits behind a faded scrim labelled INVISIBLE BY DEFAULT; three parameter chips light up one at a time (corpora=allDrives, includeItemsFromAllDrives=true, supportsAllDrives=true). Beside it, a fields= chip appears with nextPageToken called out in terracotta. THIS EXACT REQUEST RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Get the three parameters right, ask for nextPageToken, and the pages arrive complete. But now the harder failure: that spreadsheet has no downloadable bytes. A Google Sheet isn't a file — it's a live document living in Google's own store, structured, not blobbed. Ask for its bytes with alt=media and you get a flat 403, no explanation of why. The fix is the export endpoint, which materializes CSV on request. And here's the sharp edge — skip any one of these three habits and the failure never names the missing parameter. A missing supportsAllDrives comes back as a 404 that reads exactly like the file was never there. They optimized for API purity; you pay in error messages that quietly lie about which layer failed.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — complete pagination, then 403 on alt=media for a Sheet, then a missing param read back as 'not found'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — complete, then two silent failures
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 REQUEST RETURNS, identical. Pages stack up cleanly, labelled 'page 1, 2, 3 — all requested'. Beside it, two failure cards: one shows alt=media on the Sheet returning '403' in terracotta with the export endpoint marked as the fix; the other shows a missing supportsAllDrives returning '404' labelled 'looks like: never existed' — neither error names the missing parameter.

beats.narration_text: Three habits carry every Drive call Claude makes: treat a folder as a file, add supportsAllDrives for anything shared, and export — not download — for anything Google itself made. Miss one and the API lies to you about which one you missed.

props.quote: Three habits carry every Drive call: treat a folder as a file, add supportsAllDrives for anything shared, and export — not download — for anything Google itself made.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to understand how the Google Drive API handles the three edge cases that trip everyone up — shared-drive files being invisible by default, paginated results silently stopping at page one, and Google-native files like Sheets returning 403 when you ask for their bytes with alt=media. Walk me through each one: what parameter or endpoint fixes it, why the API was designed that way, and what the error looks like when you get it wrong. Then show me one Python snippet using google-api-python-client that lists every spreadsheet modified in the last thirty days on a shared drive and exports the first one as CSV — with the three shared-drive parameters, fields= including nextPageToken, and the export endpoint all used correctly. Go deeper: ask the same model why Google chose IDs over paths as Drive's addressing scheme, and what that opened up that a hierarchical filesystem couldn't.
